c.tagline: Misty tea mountains and a bamboo raft down the Nine-Bend River, where Da Hong Pao legends grow on sheer red cliffs.

card: Credit cards are rarely accepted outside a few international-standard hotels; WeChat Pay and Alipay dominate — set up mobile payment before arrival and keep some cash as backup

taxi.fareNote: Few taxis circulate — Didi is more reliable than street-hailing, especially near the scenic area entrance

emergency.note: Scenic-area staff carry radios for trail emergencies; English support is minimal — keep your hotel's number handy

walk: The scenic core is a trail-and-raft park, not a walkable city grid — you shuttle between trailheads by park bus, then hike; the low-rise city center itself is compact and easy on foot

safety.safety: Very safe, low crime, a popular domestic tea-tourism and honeymoon destination
safety.crime: Minimal — the main risk is overpaying unlicensed drivers or high-pressure tea-tasting sales pitches

hood_landmark.Wuyi Mountain Scenic Area: Tianyou Peak and the Nine-Bend River
hood_landmark.Xingcun: The original Da Hong Pao mother tea bushes
hood_landmark.Xiamei Ancient Village: Zou Family Grand House and the Meixi Canal

avoid.reason: Beware unofficial guides, bamboo-raft touts and pressure sales of overpriced 'da hong pao' tea — book rafting and park tickets through official channels.

hood_desc: The UNESCO core of red sandstone peaks and the Nine-Bend River, explored by bamboo raft and cliffside trail up to Tianyou Peak.
The modern town of Wuyi Avenue and Wuyi Square, home to the region's transit hubs, restaurants, and tea shops.
A working tea-trading town at the scenic area's southern gate, home to the original Da Hong Pao mother bushes and rows of tea-tasting houses.
Site of the 2,000-year-old Min Yue Kingdom's walled capital ruins, plus the region's biggest wholesale tea market.
A canal-laced Qing-dynasty merchant village of carved courtyard houses a short drive from town, far off the main tour-bus route.

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled water; tap water is not potable.

transit.sys: Local buses plus a free electric scenic shuttle/tram inside Wuyishan National Park
transit.pay: Cash or QR code; the scenic-area multi-day pass includes shuttle rides
transit.map: Use Amap (Gaode) or Baidu Maps and download offline
transit.note: The park shuttle bus is included in the scenic-area entrance ticket and is the main way to reach trailheads

transport.air: Wuyishan Airport (WUS), ~8 km from the city, with domestic flights to Shanghai, Beijing, Guangzhou, Xiamen, and other major cities
transport.train: Wuyishan East and Wuyishan-Beibus high-speed stations on the Hefei–Fuzhou and Nanping–Wuyishan lines — about 6 hrs from Shanghai, 3-4 hrs from Fuzhou or Xiamen
transport.bus: Regional buses link Wuyishan to Nanping, Fuzhou, and Jiangxi's Shangrao; local buses and park shuttles connect the scenic area to town
transport.ferry: None scheduled — bamboo rafting on the Nine-Bend River is recreational, not a transport link
transport.car: A car or driver is useful for reaching Xiamei Village and outlying tea plantations; the scenic area's interior is closed to private cars, shuttle only

airport.name: Wuyishan Airport
airport.distance: ~8 km (15-20 min) from Wuyishan city center
airport.transport: Taxi ~$8-10 fare into town; Didi or hotel pickup recommended given limited airport shuttle service

net.m: Solid 4G in town and along the high-speed rail corridor; weaker inside the scenic area's deeper trails
net.w: Free wifi in hotels and tea houses in town
net.ops: China Mobile, China Unicom, China Telecom
net.fwn: VPN needed for Google, WhatsApp, Instagram, and Facebook — install before arrival
net.ap: Buy a SIM or eSIM in Fuzhou or Xiamen before heading to Wuyishan; local shops have limited tourist SIM stock

tip.s: Not expected — tipping isn't part of Chinese service culture and can even confuse staff
tip.r: No tipping at restaurants; a service charge is occasionally added automatically at upscale hotel restaurants

food.name: Langu Smoked Goose (Langu Xun'e)
food.desc: Wuyishan's most famous dish: goose poached, rubbed with chilli and salt, then smoked over rice straw and torn apart by hand. A protected local speciality.

places.name: Langu Wengjia Smoked Goose
places.note: Best-known smoked goose house in town, from the Langu village tradition.

places.name: Da San Wan (Old Street branch)
places.note: Popular local restaurant serving smoked goose with Minbei home cooking.

places.name: Langu township goose stalls
places.note: The dish's home village, where families smoke geese to order.

food.name: Bamboo-Tube Rice (Zhutong Fan)
food.desc: Glutinous rice with mushroom, bacon or chestnut sealed in a fresh green bamboo section and roasted over coals until it smells of the forest.

places.name: Xingcun bamboo raft pier food street
places.note: Stalls by the raft dock cooking bamboo rice for rafters all day.

places.name: Nanyuanling village farm restaurants
places.note: Cluster of nongjiale kitchens doing bamboo rice and mountain vegetables.

places.name: Dahongpao pedestrian street
places.note: Evening food street with bamboo rice, snacks and tea shops.

food.name: Jiuqu Stream Fish (Wuyi Xiyu)
food.desc: Small fish from the Nine Bend Stream, steamed with ginger or fried crisp; sweet, clean-tasting and the classic lunch after a bamboo raft ride.

places.name: Xingcun bamboo raft pier food street
places.note: Eat the stream fish where the rafts finish, minutes from the water.

places.name: Da San Wan (Old Street branch)
places.note: Well-rated local kitchen with stream fish on the standing menu.

places.name: Nanyuanling village farm restaurants
places.note: Family restaurants cooking river fish and snails from the valley.

food.name: Hot-Spring Stewed Chicken
food.desc: Free-range mountain chicken slow-stewed with wolfberry, mushroom and sometimes rock tea leaves, a restorative served around Wuyishan's hot-spring valley.

places.name: Wuyishan hot spring resort restaurants
places.note: Spa hotels serve the chicken stew as the standard post-soak meal.

places.name: Nanyuanling village farm restaurants
places.note: Village kitchens stewing local chicken in clay pots to order.

places.name: Yan Wuyi (Impression Dahongpao branch)
places.note: Refined Minbei restaurant doing tea-and-herb chicken dishes.

food.name: Wufu Lotus Seed and Egg Custard
food.desc: White lotus seeds from Wufu town simmered with egg into a barely sweet custard; a delicate Wuyishan dessert eaten warm.

places.name: Wufu ancient town eateries
places.note: Home of the famous white lotus seed, cooked fresh in season.

places.name: Da San Wan (Old Street branch)
places.note: Serves the lotus seed custard among its regional specialities.

places.name: Dahongpao pedestrian street
places.note: Dessert and snack stalls selling lotus seed sweets in the evening.

food.name: Wengong Cai
food.desc: Layered pork-and-egg meatball dish said to date to the philosopher Zhu Xi, who taught here; a banquet staple of northern Fujian.

places.name: Yan Wuyi (Impression Dahongpao branch)
places.note: Minbei menu built around historic local dishes like Wengong cai.

places.name: Wufu ancient town eateries
places.note: Zhu Xi's own town, where the dish is still cooked for feasts.

places.name: Da San Wan (Old Street branch)
places.note: Old-street favourite for classic northern Fujian banquet plates.

food.name: Da Hong Pao Rock Tea
food.desc: The legendary Big Red Robe oolong grown on Wuyi cliffs and charcoal-roasted; mineral, toasty and steeped repeatedly in tiny gongfu cups.

places.name: Xiangjiang Mingyuan tea culture park
places.note: Large tea estate and tasting halls explaining rock-tea processing.

places.name: Tianxin Yongle Chan Temple
places.note: Monastery beside the mother trees, historically the source of Da Hong Pao.

places.name: Dahongpao pedestrian street tea houses
places.note: Row of tea shops offering free gongfu tastings before you buy.

food.name: Lapsang Souchong (Zhengshan Xiaozhong)
food.desc: The world's first black tea, smoked over pine in Tongmu village inside the Wuyi reserve; resinous and sweet, best drunk where it is made.

places.name: Tongmu village tea workshops
places.note: The birthplace of black tea; workshops let you taste straight from the roast.

places.name: Xiamei ancient village
places.note: Historic start of the tea caravan road, with old merchant tea houses.

places.name: Xiangjiang Mingyuan tea culture park
places.note: Convenient in-town tasting of both rock tea and Lapsang.

landmarks: Nine-Bend Stream (Jiuqu Xi) Bamboo Rafting
Drift on a bamboo raft down nine dreamy river bends beneath sheer sandstone cliffs, the classic way to absorb UNESCO-listed Mount Wuyi.
Tianyou Peak (Heavenly Tour Peak)
A stone stairway climbs this celebrated summit for the definitive panorama of mist-wrapped peaks curling around the Nine-Bend Stream far below.
Da Hong Pao Mother Trees
Six venerable tea bushes clinging to a sheltered cliff produce the legendary Big Red Robe oolong, once literally worth more than gold.
Wuyi Palace (Wuyigong)
A Song-dynasty Taoist palace complex at the foot of Great King Peak, gateway to ancient lanes, teahouses and memorials to philosopher Zhu Xi.
Water Curtain Cave (Shuilian Dong)
A hundred-meter waterfall veils this cliffside hollow where tea grows wild and an ancient study once hosted Confucian scholars—magical after rain.
Great King Peak (Dawang Feng)
Wuyishan's majestic sentinel monolith towers over the scenic reserve, its summit trail rewarding early hikers with sunrise views across the gorge.
Tiger Roaring Rock (Huxiao Yan)
Wind whistling through crevices gives this cliff its roaring name; carved steps pass tea terraces and the tiny Tiancheng Chan temple.
Xiamei Ancient Village
A Qing-dynasty tea-trading village of carved brick mansions along a willow-lined canal, once the starting point of the Tea Road to Russia.
Impression Da Hong Pao
Zhang Yimou's spectacular open-air night show, staged in a rotating theater with real karst peaks and tea fields as its living backdrop.
Chengcun Han City Ruins
The excavated remains of a 2,200-year-old Minyue kingdom capital, part of the UNESCO site, with a museum decoding this vanished culture.

train.note: There are no cross-border trains anywhere in Fujian, so all rail from Wuyishan is domestic. Wuyishan East station sits on the Hefei-Fuzhou high-speed railway and handles the fast G-trains (Fuzhou in about an hour, Shanghai and Hangzhou in a few hours); the older Wuyishan and Wuyishan North stations on the Hengfeng-Nanping line take slower conventional services. Buy on 12306 with your passport - the booking window opens 15 days ahead and popular trains sell out in the autumn tea and foliage season. A tram line links the high-speed station area with the Wuyishan scenic-area gate, so you rarely need a taxi.

bus.note: No international coaches serve Wuyishan; the nearest border is hundreds of kilometres away. Domestic long-distance buses use the Wuyishan bus station in Wuyishan City, with services to Nanping, Jianyang, Shangrao and Fuzhou, but high-speed rail is faster and more comfortable for almost every one of those journeys. Tickets are bought at the terminal counter (passport required) rather than online, and the last departures are early evening. Local shuttle buses connect the town, the resort district and the scenic area entrances.

ferry.note: Wuyishan is an inland mountain town with no navigable link to the sea, so there are no passenger ferries. The bamboo rafts on the Nine Bend River (Jiuqu Xi) are a sightseeing ride inside the scenic area, not transport to or from the city.

half.name: Jianyang
half.blurb: District near Wuyishan known as the birthplace of Song-dynasty Jian ware black-glazed tea bowls, with kiln sites and workshops to visit.

half.name: Jian'ou
half.blurb: Ancient walled town in Nanping with a centuries-old tea-trading history, old streets, and the historic Beiyuan tea gardens nearby.

half.name: Zhenghe County
half.blurb: Rural county famous for white tea production and covered wooden bridges spanning its rivers.
